grammar.title: Singular and plural nouns
grammar.intro: A singular countable noun names one item. A plural names more than one. Choose the noun form and the words around it together.

content.title: One item and more than one
content.formation: Use a determiner with an ordinary singular countable noun. Plurals usually add -s.

examples.en: A visitor is waiting. Three visitors are waiting.
My notebook is on the desk. Our notebooks are in the bag.

content.title: Regular spelling changes
content.formation: Add -es after common sibilant endings: -s, -ss, -sh, -ch and -x. A consonant + y changes to -ies; a vowel + y usually takes -s.

examples.en: one dish → two dishes; one match → four matches
one city → several cities; one key → several keys

notes: Some -o nouns add -es, such as tomatoes; others add -s, such as photos. Check a dictionary.

content.title: Irregular and unchanged plurals
content.formation: Learn irregular forms as word pairs. Some countable nouns keep the same form in singular and plural.

examples.en: one child → three children; one tooth → two teeth
one sheep is outside. Six sheep are outside.

notes: Some -f/-fe nouns change to -ves: leaf/leaves, knife/knives. Others do not: roof/roofs, belief/beliefs.

content.title: Plural is different from possession
content.formation: An ordinary plural has no apostrophe. Use an apostrophe to mark possession, not to make more than one.

examples.en: The teachers are here. The teacher’s bag is here.
These shoes are new. This shoe is new.

notes: The plural of person is usually people when referring to individuals. People can also name a population: the peoples of a region.

grammar.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
grammar.intro: Countability concerns the meaning of a noun in a particular sentence. It affects articles, quantities and verb agreement.

content.title: Count individual items
content.formation: Countable nouns allow a/an in the singular and numbers in the plural.

examples.en: We need a chair and two lamps.
There is an envelope beside the door.

content.title: Measure an amount
content.formation: Uncountable meanings normally have no ordinary plural and use a singular verb. Add a unit when you need a count.

examples.en: This equipment is heavy. These two pieces of equipment are heavy.
There is useful information in the email.

notes: Advice, furniture, luggage and homework are normally uncountable in everyday English. Say a piece of advice, an item of furniture, a bag or an assignment.

content.title: Meaning can change the pattern
content.formation: The same word may name a substance, an individual item, a serving or a type.

examples.en: We need some paper for the printer. She presented two research papers.
Coffee keeps me awake. Two coffees, please: two cups of coffee.

notes: A pair of trousers is one item of clothing; the trousers are on the chair. A pair takes a singular verb, while trousers takes a plural verb.

grammar.title: Subject and verb agreement
grammar.intro: The subject determines the verb form. Find the head of the subject phrase before looking at nearby nouns.

content.title: Match the subject, not the nearest noun
content.formation: Use a singular verb with a singular subject and a plural verb with a plural subject. A phrase with of, with or near does not normally change the subject’s number.

examples.en: The box of cables is under the table.
The cables in that box are damaged.

content.title: Each, every and two subjects
content.formation: Each and every normally introduce a singular subject. Two separate people or things joined by and normally take a plural verb.

examples.en: Every student has a locker. Each answer needs a reason.
The designer and the editor work together.

notes: A single combined item or activity can take a singular verb: Bread and butter is my usual breakfast. Meaning matters.

content.title: Questions and negative sentences
content.formation: Does/did already carry the tense or agreement marking; the following main verb uses its base form.

examples.en: Sara works here. Does Sara work here? Sara does not work here.
The volunteers arrive early. Do the volunteers arrive early?

grammar.title: Quantities: some, any, much and many
grammar.intro: Choose quantity expressions according to countability and the meaning you want to communicate.

content.title: Many / much / a lot of
content.formation: Use many with plural countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns. A lot of works with either.

examples.en: We do not have many seats or much space.
The workshop attracted a lot of visitors and a lot of interest.

content.title: Some and any
content.formation: Some is common in affirmative statements and offers. Any is common in negatives and open questions.

examples.en: There are some oranges, but there is not any juice.
Would you like some water? Do you have any questions?

notes: These are common patterns, not absolute rules. Any can also mean it does not matter which: Choose any seat.

content.title: A few / few and a little / little
content.formation: A few and a little present an available amount. Few and little often stress that the amount is disappointingly small.

examples.en: We have a few volunteers, enough to run the event. We have few volunteers, so the event may be cancelled.
There is a little milk left, enough for your tea.

notes: A few/few go with plural countable nouns. A little/little go with uncountable nouns. Enough goes before a noun: enough chairs.

grammar.title: Adverbs of frequency
grammar.intro: Frequency words describe how often something happens. Choose their position around the verb, not just the word itself.

content.title: Before an ordinary main verb
content.formation: Subject + frequency adverb + main verb.

examples.en: Mina usually walks to her lesson.
We sometimes practise after dinner.

notes: Always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely and never describe different frequencies. Never already has a negative meaning.

content.title: After be; inside an auxiliary phrase
content.formation: Subject + be + adverb. With an auxiliary, the adverb usually follows the first auxiliary.

examples.en: The classroom is often quiet.
I have never visited that library.

notes: Do not add not to never: I never skip breakfast. Sometimes can also occur at the start or end of a clause.

content.title: Say how many times
content.formation: Once / twice / three times + a day, week or month.

examples.en: I review my notes twice a week.
How often do you practise speaking?

notes: Every Monday needs no time preposition. Use a frequency phrase to make a study routine specific.

grammar.title: Time prepositions: at, on and in
grammar.intro: Use a time preposition to connect an event with a clock time, a day or a longer period. Some common time phrases have no preposition.

content.title: Clock times and familiar expressions
content.formation: At + clock time; at noon, at night and at the weekend in British English.

examples.en: The conversation class starts at 7.15.
We usually read at night.

notes: At the weekend is common in British English; on the weekend is common in American English. Both varieties are valid.

content.title: Days and specific dates
content.formation: On + day or date; on + a specific day and part of the day.

examples.en: Our group meets on Thursday.
The interview is on Monday morning.

notes: A named day makes the time specific: on Friday evening, but in the evening.

content.title: Longer periods and no-preposition phrases
content.formation: In + month, season, year or general part of the day. No preposition before next, last, this or every.

examples.en: My new course begins in September.
We meet next Tuesday and practise every morning.

notes: In winter describes a season; the weather depends on the place and hemisphere.

grammar.title: Verbs followed by -ing or to + verb
grammar.intro: When one verb follows another, the first verb often controls the form of the second. Learn the complete pattern in a meaningful sentence.

source.title: British Council: Verbs followed by -ing or infinitive

content.title: Enjoy, avoid and finish
content.formation: Enjoy / avoid / finish + verb-ing.

examples.en: I enjoy discussing films with my friends.
She finished writing her message.

notes: The -ing form can act as the object of a verb. Do not insert to after enjoy.

content.title: Want, decide and hope
content.formation: Want / decide / hope + to + base verb.

examples.en: We decided to practise in the library.
I hope to understand the next conversation.

notes: To is followed by the base form, not an -ing form, in these patterns.

content.title: Some verbs allow both patterns
content.formation: Like and love can often be followed by -ing or to + verb; would like uses to + verb.

examples.en: I like reading on the train.
I would like to join the discussion.

notes: Some pattern changes also change meaning. Learn a new verb with its example rather than guessing from translation.

grammar.title: Enough and too
grammar.intro: Enough describes a sufficient amount or degree for a purpose. Too describes an amount or degree beyond what is wanted or suitable.

content.title: Enough with a noun
content.formation: Enough + noun; not enough + noun.

examples.en: We have enough chairs for the group.
There is not enough time to review every answer.

notes: Enough comes before countable plural and uncountable nouns.

content.title: Enough after an adjective or adverb
content.formation: Adjective / adverb + enough + to + verb.

examples.en: The room is quiet enough to record in.
Please speak slowly enough for me to take notes.

notes: The purpose matters: loud enough to hear and too loud to concentrate describe different limits.

content.title: Too is different from very
content.formation: Too + adjective; too much + uncountable noun; too many + plural countable noun.

examples.en: The recording is too fast for me to follow.
There are too many examples on this small card.

notes: Very describes a high degree. Too expresses an excessive degree in relation to a need or purpose.

grammar.title: Present perfect: results and activity
grammar.intro: Both forms connect the past with now. The simple often presents a result or number; the continuous often highlights activity, duration or recent evidence.

source.title: British Council: Present perfect simple and continuous

content.title: A completed result or number
content.formation: Have / has + past participle.

examples.en: I have answered six questions, so I can take a break.
She has sent the message; it is in your inbox.

notes: A stated count of completed actions often favours the simple form.

content.title: An activity or its duration
content.formation: Have / has + been + verb-ing.

examples.en: I have been practising for twenty minutes and I am still working.
His hands are dirty because he has been repairing his bike.

notes: The activity may still be continuing or may have just stopped. Context establishes whether it is finished.

content.title: Choose by meaning, not a signal word alone
content.formation: Some state verbs normally use the simple form. Some situations permit both forms with a different focus.

examples.en: I have known my classmate for a year.
We have lived here for years. We have been living here for years.

notes: For and since can occur with both forms. Do not mark one form wrong when the context genuinely supports both.

grammar.title: Past habits: used to and would
grammar.intro: Used to can contrast past habits or states with now. Would can describe repeated past actions when a past context has already been established.

content.title: A past habit or state that changed
content.formation: Used to + base verb.

examples.en: I used to live near the station, but now I live outside town.
We used to practise on paper before we had a computer.

notes: Used to can describe states such as live, know and own as well as repeated actions.

content.title: Repeated past actions with would
content.formation: Past context + would + base verb.

examples.en: When I was at school, we would read together after lunch.
During that summer, my cousin would call every Friday.

notes: For a past state, used to is normally the suitable choice. The past simple can also describe past habits.

content.title: Questions and negatives
content.formation: Did + subject + use to …? Subject + did not + use to …

examples.en: Did you use to study with that group?
I did not use to take notes, but I do now.

notes: After did, use the base form use. Be used to + noun/-ing means accustomed to and is a different pattern.
